name: LoRA AI Toolkit WAN 2.2
subcategory: LoRA training and inference for video models
tagline: A hosted toolkit for training LoRAs on the Wan 2.2 video model and generating clips with them.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Every load bearing piece here is open: Wan 2.2 weights are public, and the training scripts people actually use for video LoRAs are community projects. So an agent can absolutely build you a local job queue, a dataset prep step, a training runner and a generate page in one long session. What it cannot build you is a GPU. This category lives and dies on VRAM and hours, and a hosted toolkit is mostly selling you working defaults plus somebody else's hardware, which is a real thing to sell. Build it if you already own a fat card or are happy renting one by the hour, otherwise the DIY version is a very nice UI in front of an out of memory error.
coreLoopDIY: Upload a folder of clips or stills, auto caption and bucket them, kick off a Wan 2.2 LoRA training run in a local queue, then generate test videos with the resulting LoRA at chosen strength.
requirements: An NVIDIA GPU with 24GB VRAM or more, or a rented cloud GPU
Wan 2.2 base weights pulled from Hugging Face, plus roughly 100GB of free disk
CUDA and Python toolchain patience: version pinning is most of the pain
A dataset you actually have the rights to train on
whatYouLose: Somebody else's tuned hyperparameters, which is most of what you are paying for
Instant capacity: no queue jumping, no second run while the first one is training
Preset pipelines and model version upgrades handled for you when Wan ships a new checkpoint
A gallery, sharing, and any way to hand a LoRA to a collaborator
Recovery when a 6 hour run dies at hour 5 and you have no idea why
moatNotes: The weights are open and the trainers are open. The scarce things are GPU hours and a config that does not diverge.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because renting the hardware and getting the training config right are both annoying in ways that do not make you better at anything. A hosted toolkit turns a weekend of dependency archaeology into a form upload, and when a new Wan checkpoint lands it keeps working without you rebuilding your environment. If you train LoRAs occasionally rather than constantly, paying per run is genuinely cheaper than owning a card that idles.
notes: The software is a weekend; the GPU bill is forever.
prompt:
Build a local, single user web app for training and using LoRAs on the Wan 2.2 video model. Empty folder, no cloud services, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, FastAPI, Jinja2 templates plus htmx for the UI. No React.
- SQLite via sqlite3 for jobs and metadata. No ORM.
- Background work runs in a single worker process that polls the jobs table. One job at a time, because there is one GPU.
- Training delegates to an existing Wan 2.2 LoRA trainer CLI (musubi-tuner style) invoked as a subprocess. Do not write a trainer from scratch. Put the command template in config.toml so I can swap it.
- Inference delegates to a Wan 2.2 text-to-video / image-to-video script, also a subprocess with a template in config.toml.

Features in scope:
1. Datasets page: create a dataset, drag in images or short clips, they land in data/datasets/NAME/. Show thumbnails and a caption box per item. A "auto caption" button that runs a local captioner if available and otherwise leaves captions blank.
2. Training page: pick a dataset, set rank, learning rate, steps, resolution bucket, and output name. Submit creates a queued job row. Show live tail of the trainer stdout via a polling htmx endpoint reading the job log file.
3. LoRAs page: list finished .safetensors in data/loras/ with the config used, step count, and wall clock time.
4. Generate page: prompt, optional init image, LoRA picker with strength slider, frame count, steps, seed. Queues an inference job, shows the resulting mp4 inline when done.
5. Jobs page: queued / running / failed / done, cancel button that kills the subprocess group, and the last 200 log lines on failure.

Out of scope, do not build: user accounts, billing, multi tenancy, GPU autoscaling, remote workers, a mobile app, any hosted storage.

Rules: model weights path, HF token and output dirs come from .env, and ship .env.example. Write a README with exact install steps, the VRAM floor, and a note that dependency versions are pinned in requirements.txt for a reason. If the GPU is missing, the app must still start and say so plainly instead of crashing.
